filled_passage:
I volunteered to draw a visitor map for a community garden. A page, a ruler and a list of attractions seemed enough. I wanted a map that would make the garden look simple, so I marked the shortest route between the entrance and each feature.

Most visitors followed my arrows easily, giving me confidence in the design. Then a woman using a walking frame stopped at a narrow turn. She could see the pond, but she could not comfortably reach it by the route I had recommended. I showed her a longer path. “That works,” she said, “but your map makes it look like the wrong way.”

I had treated distance as the only measure of convenience. The longer route had a smoother surface and more space at the corners, details I had left out because they did not fit my simple scheme. I was ready to mark that route for everyone. Our teacher asked whether I was replacing one assumption with another.

The following weekend, we asked visitors to compare two draft maps. Some preferred the short path; others valued a place to sit halfway round. One parent wanted a quieter place for her child. The answers did not reveal a single perfect route. They showed that a useful map might need to offer alternatives rather than quietly choose for its readers.

We checked the paths with the garden staff and described their surfaces and resting places. A narrow section remained unchecked after rain. We left a gap rather than guess at its condition. I disliked the unfinished appearance, but a note made the missing information explicit. It was better than allowing a neat line to create false certainty.

Before printing, the woman tried the revision and suggested enlarging one label. She was not approving it for all visitors; she offered her own perspective. Others contributed theirs.

The final map was less elegant than my first drawing. It was also more informative. Two families took different routes without seeming lost. What I had first regarded as a failure to give clear directions was now a way to respect different needs.

I still cared about the map's appearance, but I no longer wanted its simplicity to conceal the garden's complexity. A good design could acknowledge uncertainty without becoming useless. It could invite a decision rather than impose one. Further checks let us fill the blank. I kept the old draft, not as an example to imitate, but as a reminder to ask: what have we made easy to see, and what have we overlooked? The route I had once considered a detour became part of the main map. Our task had changed from directing an average visitor to assisting real people in making their own choices. That required more listening, and less certainty about what everybody wanted.
